_about: Hand-written source facts per plate, merged with the measured geometry by build-json.py into src/data/plates.json. 'date' is the publication date shown on or stated by the page; 'licence' is as stated on the page on the day it was read, or 'none stated'. 'label' is a suggested on-screen source line (Decision 11 wording for individuals).

A2-01.source: arXiv 2610.27381, W. De Michele and K. Tantithamthavorn, "Documentation Drift in AI-Generated Pull Requests" (Accepted at APSEC 2026, Early Research Achievements)
A2-01.label: arXiv, Oct 2026
A2-01.dateNote: Submitted 19 Oct 2026 (v1), shown on the page
A2-01.text: We find that 63.2% of AI PRs change code without updating any documentation.
A2-01.licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (licence link on the abstract page: creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
notes: 'Documentation' here means documentation files in the same repository, not Confluence pages.
CC BY-SA: the processed plate is an adaptation; publish it under CC BY-SA with attribution if the plate files are shared.

D1-04.text: Secondly, throw away your runbooks. They are out of date the moment you hit save.

D1-11.source: Wednesday Wisdom (Substack), "The loneliness of the long distance runbook"
D1-11.label: Wednesday Wisdom (blog), 2024
D1-11.dateNote: Shown under the post title as "DEC 11, 2024"
D1-11.text: In a more than completely static environment, runbooks are always out of date. There is unfortunately nothing to be done about that, just live with it!
notes: The author is an individual; the plate shows the paragraph only (no name, photo or masthead). Label it with the publication name.

D1-21.source: Hacker News comment (handle blurred), thread "We should revisit literate programming in the agent era"
D1-21.label: Hacker News comment, 2026
D1-21.dateNote: Shown on the page as a relative age ("8 months ago"); exact date from the item's timestamp
D1-21.text: Documentation rots a lot more quickly than the code - it doesn't need to be correct for the code to work.
notes: The comment's second sentence advises ignoring docs and reading the code; the crop ends in the space before it.
The handle in the comment header is blurred; the header still shows the age ("8 months ago") and the thread title.

D1-12.label: Simon Willison's Weblog, 2022
D1-12.text: If your docs live in a separate wiki somewhere it’s easy for them to get out of date—but more importantly it’s hard for anyone to quickly confirm if the documentation is being updated in sync with the code or not.
notes: His answer is to keep docs in the repository; we answer the case where they are not. No endorsement implied.

A1-13.source: arXiv 2609.31342, M. S. Ahmed, L. G. Poech and R. Röttger, "Stale-Document Poisoning: When Outdated Retrieval Overrides Correct Model Answers" (preprint)
A1-13.label: arXiv, Sep 2026
A1-13.dateNote: Submitted 25 Sep 2026, shown on the page
A1-13.text: More importantly, outdated retrieval flips 30% of Llama and 37% of Qwen answers even without instructions to trust the document; explicit follow instructions raise these rates to 66% and 75%.

A2-02.text: As preliminary evidence, applying an existing README/wiki consistency checker to a statistically representative sample of 356 repositories identifies stale code element references in 23.0% of repositories, showing that traditional documentation consistency tools can already surface context rot.
